title: Vaisakhi: the harvest
hookLine: a spring harvest day in Punjab that became the birthday of the Khalsa in 1699
last: SANGAT — SIT, EAT, GO IN PEACE.

cards: In Punjab, in April, the wheat turns gold. For months the fields have been green, and then, almost at once, they're the color of bread. Farmers who've watched the sky all winter can finally breathe: the crop is in.

So, for centuries, there's been a festival: drums, bhangra dancing in the fields, fairs, new clothes, sweets. Punjabis of every faith celebrate it. But for Sikhs, this harvest day holds something else too.
On one Vaisakhi, more than three hundred years ago, something was born.

teach.b: Vaisakhi is the first day of Vaisakh, a month in the Indian solar calendar, and it usually falls on the thirteenth or fourteenth of April.
In Punjab it's been the harvest day for a very long time: the spring wheat is ready, the sickles come out, the villages celebrate. The Gurus used this gathering.
Guru Amar Das asked Sikhs to come to him at Vaisakhi, and it became a day when the scattered sangat met.
Then, in 1699, at Anandpur, Guru Gobind Singh used that same gathering for the call you heard back on day eighty-four: the five beloved, the amrit, the birth of the Khalsa. No retelling today.
Just notice where it landed: on a harvest day. And the harvest is a picture the Gurus had used all along.
Guru Nanak spent his last years farming at Kartarpur, and in one of his hymns he turns a whole farmer's year inward.

teach.h: THE MIND AS PLOWMAN, THE NAME AS SEED.
teach.b: In paraphrase: make your mind the plowman and good deeds the farming, let effort be the water and your body the field.

teach.h: THE END OF GROWING, A NEW SEED.
teach.b: Sow the Name as the seed, level the ground with contentment, and keep humility as the fence around it. Then, by grace, the crop comes up.

So the Khalsa can be heard as a harvest: two centuries of the Gurus' patient sowing, since Guru Nanak, coming in all at once. And a harvest is also a beginning, because next year's seed comes out of it.
That's why Sikhs celebrate both together: harvest and birth. Wherever Sikhs live now, Vaisakhi is one of the biggest days of the year.

how: Sikhs celebrate Vaisakhi, usually on April 13 or 14, with services at the gurdwara, an akhand path, amrit ceremonies, the renewal of the Nishan Sahib, nagar kirtan processions and langar, alongside Punjab's harvest festivities.

games.q: Guru Nanak pictures a life as a farm: the mind is the plowman, the body is the field. what does he make the seed?
games.why: sow the Name as the seed, he says, with contentment to level the ground and humility as the fence.

practice: If you can, look out of a window or step outside, and find something growing or resting, whatever the season where you are: a tree, a weed in the sidewalk, a plant on a shelf, even the grass. Look at it for a moment.
Then turn inward: what's been growing slowly in your own life, is any of it ready, and what might be starting right at the end of something?

wordCard.voice: Vaisakhi. The spring harvest day in Punjab, in mid-April, which in 1699 became the birthday of the Khalsa.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Vaisakhi, often spelled Baisakhi, the first day of Vaisakh.
